title: The Orthodox Church
hook: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy and becoming like God by grace

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was schism: 1054, when East and West tore apart. Your line was the split still aches.

Around the year 987, an old chronicle from Kyiv says, Prince Vladimir sent envoys out to see how different peoples worshiped. Back from Constantinople, from the great church of Hagia Sophia, they could hardly describe it. They said, more or less: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people. The gold, the singing, the incense rising through light from high windows. Soon after, Vladimir was baptized, and with him the people of Kyiv. Step inside an Orthodox church today, Greek, Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Ukrainian, and some visitors still describe what those envoys described. Candles flickering before painted faces. People kissing pictures. Many standing.

Orthodoxy is Greek: orthos, right or straight, and doxa, which means both belief and glory. So: right belief, and right worship, or praise. Orthodox Christians would say you can't separate the two: what you believe is how you pray. The Orthodox Church is a family of self-governing churches, the patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and the churches of Russia, Greece, Romania, Serbia and more, sharing one faith and one communion, with no single head. Its main service is the Divine Liturgy, most often the one named for Saint John Chrysostom, sung almost entirely. Icons fill the church: Christ, Mary, the saints. Kissing an icon isn't worshiping wood and paint. A council in 787 said the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love. And the goal of it all has a surprising name: theosis, becoming like God. It's rooted in a line from Second Peter, that we might be "partakers of the divine nature." Early church fathers went further: God became human so that humans might share God's life. The Orthodox are careful here: not by nature, as if people turn into gods, but by grace, the way iron left in a fire glows with the fire's heat while staying iron. This week's arc: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of Africa and Asia; the road east; 1054; and now worship as heaven on earth.
screen: `ORTHOS AND DOXA: RIGHT PRAISE.` · `A FAMILY OF CHURCHES, ONE FAITH.` · `THE HONOR PASSES TO THE ONE SHOWN.` · `THEOSIS: IRON GLOWING IN FIRE.` · then, large: `PARTAKERS OF THE DIVINE NATURE.`

segments.voice: Light a candle before a holy picture, or a photograph of someone you love; if you can't light a flame, picture one. Look at the face, and let the honor you feel pass through the picture to the person it shows. If you pray, pray the way Orthodox Christians do before icons, silently, simply, eyes open; if you don't, just keep looking with love.
Orthodoxy. Right belief and right praise, from the Greek orthos and doxa. The church of icons and the Divine Liturgy.
Your line: heaven on earth. For the Orthodox, what you believe is how you pray. Day two hundred eighty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians often keep an icon corner at home with a small lamp, cross themselves and kiss the icons when they enter church, and stand through a Divine Liturgy that is sung from start to finish.

fork.setup: you walk into an Orthodox church and see an old woman kiss a painting of Christ. what is she doing, in the church's own words?
options: honoring Christ, the one the painting shows.

original.note: Greek: orthos, right, and doxa, belief and glory. Right belief, and right praise.

trapdoor: what you thought: orthodox means strict, or old-fashioned.
what it means: right belief and right praise, the name of a family of churches whose worship is meant to be heaven on earth.
what a scholar hears: doxa, the same word as in doxology. and theosis: sharing God's life by grace, as iron glows in fire.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): hook no longer opens a sentence with 'Walk into' or tells the listener what they'll feel; 'almost everyone standing' softened.

Vladimir's envoys: from the Primary Chronicle (entry for 987), paraphrased. The chronicle also describes envoys to other faiths; the script leaves that out to avoid comparison. Baptism of Kyiv c. 988.
List of Orthodox churches is partial; the status of some (e.g. the Orthodox Church of Ukraine) is disputed among Orthodox churches — script avoids naming it as a separate church.
Iron-in-fire image for theosis: traditional (e.g. Maximus the Confessor, John of Damascus). Confirm attribution is not needed.
Athanasius's line ('He was made man that we might be made God') paraphrased as 'God became human so that humans might share God's life'. Confirm.
